**August 24, 1931 — a Monday**

You were born at the bottom of the world's economic collapse, into a year that felt like it might not end well for anyone.

The Great Depression was not yet two years old, but it had already done enormous damage. Thousands of American banks had failed. Unemployment was climbing past 15 percent and still rising — it would reach 25 percent by 1933. Breadlines were a fixture of American cities. The global trading system had fractured. Governments everywhere were scrambling, mostly unsuccessfully, to find solid ground.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, the British government fell.

Ramsay MacDonald, the Labour Prime Minister, had spent weeks trying to hold his Cabinet together over a proposed cut to unemployment benefits — demanded by creditors as the price of a financial rescue. The Cabinet split and couldn't agree. On August 24, MacDonald went to Buckingham Palace and resigned. King George V asked him to stay on — not as a Labour leader but as the head of a new National Government, a coalition of Conservatives, Liberals, and a rump of Labour. MacDonald agreed.

The Labour Party called it a betrayal. Most of his Cabinet refused to join. MacDonald was expelled from the party he had helped found. The National Government pushed through the austerity measures, Britain abandoned the gold standard the following month, and the economic crisis ground on regardless.

It was a moment that captured what 1931 felt like: institutions under pressure making desperate choices, with no clear sense of what would actually work. The political and economic ground was shifting in ways that nobody had a reliable map for.

---

**Three months before your birth**, the Empire State Building opened in New York City. It was the tallest structure humans had ever built — 102 floors, 1,454 feet to the top of the antenna — and it had been constructed in just 410 days. It was also, by the time it opened, a near-empty monument to the decade that had just ended. Most of its office space went unleased for years. New Yorkers called it the Empty State Building. It stood as a strange symbol of what the 1920s had imagined the future would look like, completed precisely as that future was foreclosed.

---

**What was coming** in the weeks and months after you were born is more ominous than what happened on the day itself.

Twenty-five days after your birth, on September 18, Japanese military officers staged an incident on a railway line in Manchuria and used it as a pretext to invade the region. The Mukden Incident was the opening move of a Japanese imperial expansion that would eventually drag the entire Pacific into war. The League of Nations issued reports. Nothing happened. The lesson — that international institutions would not stop a determined aggressor — was absorbed and remembered.

Seventeen months after your birth, Adolf Hitler became Chancellor of Germany.

You entered a world that had not yet reckoned with either of those facts.

---

**You are 95 years old.**

That number deserves a moment. You were born before the New Deal existed, before the atom bomb existed, before television was in homes, before antibiotics were widely available, before commercial aviation was routine, before the United Nations, before NATO, before the interstate highway system, before the computer. You have seen every one of those things arrive.

You were ten years old when Pearl Harbor was attacked — old enough to understand what it meant, young enough that you wouldn't be sent to the Pacific. You were a teenager through the war, a young adult in the postwar boom, in your thirties during the civil rights movement and the Kennedy years. You were 38 when Apollo 11 landed on the moon. You watched the Berlin Wall fall at 58, and the Soviet Union dissolve the following year. You were 70 on September 11, 2001.

The world you were born into had no reliable treatment for tuberculosis, no polio vaccine, and an economy in free fall. The dominant mass medium was radio. A long-distance telephone call required an operator and planning in advance. The photograph was roughly 90 years old. Human flight was 28 years old.

You have now lived long enough to hold a pocket-sized device that contains more accumulated human knowledge than any library that existed when you were born, connected in real time to every other such device on Earth.

The summer of 1931 was not a summer anyone who lived through it remembered with fondness. It was frightened and uncertain, the Depression at its grip and worse things still coming. Whatever kind of world you entered that August Monday, it was not an easy one. That you have moved through 95 years of its history is, by any measure, an extraordinary thing.
